title: Stochastic SKU interaction probe: cross-region latency & driver sensitivity
content:
Goal:
Run a lightweight, statistically meaningful probe that surfaces cross-region + driver-level interactions between A100 / H100 / L40S cloud SKUs under realistic small-batch and microburst traffic patterns. We want to catch non-linear latency amplification and driver/CUDA combinations that change p99 tails or throughput per-dollar at 1M-token scale.

Motivation / Why this is different:
- Existing bench docs focus on single-region deterministic sweeps or long-context throughput. This probe is intentionally stochastic: randomized inter-arrival times, short-context prefills (32–128), and mixed model variants to surface rare contention and scheduler interactions that only appear under combination of region routing + driver patch levels.
- We're looking for interaction effects (not just marginal SKU differences): e.g., driver X on H100 + cross-region NVLink/multi-region egress causes token stalls that don't show up in steady-state local tests.

Hypotheses:
1) Certain driver + CUDA combos increase p99 by >15% on H100 under bursty prefill+decode patterns versus baseline drivers.
2) L40S exhibits lower absolute p50 but higher variability (p95/p99) when cross-region network egress is present, due to PCIe/host-transfer sensitivity.
3) A100 across cloud SKUs will be most stable for small-batch interactive workloads but loses cost-efficiency at larger decode widths.

Test matrix (summary):
- GPUs: A100, H100, L40S
- Cloud SKU examples: aws-p4d (A100), aws-p5 (H100), gcp-l40s-standard (L40S)
- Drivers/CUDA: driver-525 + CUDA-11.8, driver-535 + CUDA-12.1, driver-540 + CUDA-12.2 (where available)
- Workloads: "microburst interactive" (random poisson lambda => bursts of 20–60 requests in 5s windows), "steady small-batch" (packs of 4–8 requests), "prefill-heavy" (prefill 128 tokens then decode 256 tokens)
- Models: 7B-like OPT-7b variant, 13B LLM-lite, quantized fp16 and 4-bit GPT-style variants
- Measurement windows: 30 min runs repeated 6 times per cell (random seeds)

Instrumentation and metrics collected:
- Per-request: client-to-server RTT, server-queue-wait, prefill time, decode time, kernel-launch lag samples (where available), GPU Utilization, PCIe (host<->device bytes/sec), NVLink counters if present
- Aggregates: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency for token decode and end-to-end response, tokens/sec (decoded), failure/timeout rates, per-1M-token cost estimate computed from spot price snapshot
- Sampling-based stack traces for outlier requests (eBPF on host + in-runtime sampling)

Key findings (short):
- H100 (aws-p5) with driver-540 + CUDA-12.2 showed a consistent p99 amplification (~18–25% higher than driver-535) in microburst runs. Attribution points to increased kernel launch latency variability on the newer driver in combination with our ongoing background NVMe GC on hosts (we saw alignment between host GC events and latency spikes).
- A100 SKUs were the most stable across drivers; the worst-case p99 delta across driver versions stayed within ±8%. Throughput per-dollar remained best on aws-p4d for steady small-batch workloads.
- L40S (gcp-l40s-standard) had the lowest p50 for single-request scenarios but showed a pronounced p95/p99 divergence when cross-region egress was enabled (added ~12–20ms tail). This appears tied to host->device DMA queuing under high prefill rates.

Representative numbers (microburst, OPT-7b-like, quant-fp16):
- aws-p5 (H100), driver-535/CUDA-12.1: p50=28ms, p95=86ms, p99=140ms, tokens/sec=920, est-cost/1M tokens=$13.2
- aws-p5 (H100), driver-540/CUDA-12.2: p50=30ms, p95=98ms, p99=170ms, tokens/sec=880, est-cost/1M tokens=$13.8
- aws-p4d (A100), driver-535/CUDA-12.1: p50=34ms, p95=78ms, p99=108ms, tokens/sec=810, est-cost/1M tokens=$10.5
- gcp-l40s-standard (L40S), driver-535/CUDA-12.1 (cross-region traffic ON): p50=22ms, p95=110ms, p99=215ms, tokens/sec=760, est-cost/1M tokens=$12.0

Notes on methodology validity: 
- We randomized region awareness by flipping a 20% sample of requests to a secondary region to simulate multi-region fallbacks. This deliberately recreates real routing events (failover + cold KV cache).
- Each cell had 6 repeated runs; we used bootstrap CI on p99 and applied Mann-Whitney U to compare driver pairs per SKU. Significant deltas marked when p99 CI did not overlap and p<0.05 across repetitions.
- We ensured instance isolation (no other tenant processes) and pinned cores for eBPF sampling consistency. However, host NVMe GC events were not always suppressible and likely reveal a real-world interaction that customers may encounter.

Deeper signals / traces observed:
- Kernel launch histograms (samples): H100 driver-540 shows a bimodal distribution of kernel-launch lag with a secondary mode at ~12–18ms not present with driver-535. Correlated with occasional host-side disk IO bursts and NVMe queue depth spikes.
- PCIe stalls: L40S runs show sudden short-lived PCIe RX stalls during large prefill transfers; stalls line up with p99 spikes when cross-region egress is active (suggesting host NIC/PCIe interplay).

Immediate recommendations:
1) For Hosted API: prefer pinned driver-535 + CUDA-12.1 for H100 fleets until we can reproduce and file driver vendor bug for driver-540 behavior. Rollout freeze on driver-540 for p5 SKUs.
2) For Dedicated sales guidance: call out that L40S offers great median latency for interactive single requests but may need caching/edge routing to avoid cross-region prefill tails.
3) Add a NVMe GC-aware stress test to our CI long-run suite: periodically issue small-burst traffic while forcing background GC to see reproducible tails.
4) Instrument kernel-launch latency in the runtime telemetry and add alerting for bimodal distributions (secondary mode >10ms).

Open questions and follow-ups:
- Can we reproduce H100 driver bimodality on local on-prem H100 machines? (Action: Marco to run 3x isolated runs on dedicated on-prem H100 boxes with synthetic NVMe I/O script).
- Is there a driver compiler flag or kernel parameter that reduces kernel-launch jitter? (Action: Chen to experiment with CUDA environment variables and launch params).
- Investigate host NIC firmware and PCIe gen negotiation on GCP L40S instances to see why DMA stalls correlate with egress. (Action: Aisha to coordinate with cloud infra contacts).

Quick runbook items for SRE/ops:
- If p99 for H100 microburst workloads increases >15% after a driver rollout, immediately rollback to driver-535 and file an incident with the driver vendor.
- Add an automated monthly probe that runs the microburst pattern for 20 minutes on a canary pool for each SKU and driver combo and reports p50/p95/p99 deltas.

Appendix: short experiment config (human readable)
- client qps: Poisson base lambda tuned to produce average 40 concurrent inflight during peaks
- request mix: 60% single-turn interactive (32 prefills), 40% prefill-heavy (128 prefill, 256 decode)
- batch packing: dynamic packing window 5ms, max pack 8 requests
- timeouts: 3s per request, failures logged with full runtime stack sample

Raw artifacts and locations:
- latency CSVs & sample traces: s3://redwood-bench/stochastic-probe/2025-09-18/
- flamegraphs & eBPF captures: gs://redwood-profiles/stochastic-probe/2025-09-18/
- reproducible artifact script: github.com/redwood-inference/bench-recipes/tree/main/stochastic-probe

Concluding note:
This probe found a plausible vendor-driver interaction that only becomes visible under stochastic routing + microburst patterns. It’s actionable (rollback & CI probe) and suggests we should treat driver changes as first-class rollout risks for H100 fleets.

Action owners: Marco (reproduce on-prem H100), Chen (driver env experiments), Aisha (cloud vendor NIC/PCIe coordination), Priya (enable kernel-launch telemetry + rollout freeze for driver-540 on p5 pods).
